title: Ethics: Happiness, Virtue and the Golden Mean
subtitle: What a whole human life is for, and how good character is built one habit at a time
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what Aristotle meant by eudaimonia and why it is not the same as feeling happy
Reconstruct the function argument and identify its most serious weakness
Explain how virtues of character are formed by habit and why each lies in a 'mean relative to us'
Describe practical wisdom (phronesis) and its role in good action
Distinguish Aristotle's three kinds of friendship and apply them to your own relationships
hook:
Imagine two lives. In the first, a person is plugged into perfect pleasures every day: delicious food, flattering company, endless entertainment. They never accomplish anything, never face a hard choice, never really know anyone. In the second, a person works at something difficult that they care about, keeps a few deep friendships, faces some losses with courage and grows wiser with age. Both say, if asked, that they are 'happy'. Is one of them actually living better?

Most people feel the second life is better, even if the first is more pleasant. Aristotle thought that feeling points to something true. In a set of lectures given at his school, the Lyceum, and later edited as the *Nicomachean Ethics* (probably named after his son Nicomachus, who may have edited them), he built the most influential account in history of what a good human life is. It begins with a deceptively simple question: what is everything we do ultimately *for*?

sections.heading: The Highest Good: Eudaimonia
sections.body:
The *Nicomachean Ethics* opens with a sentence that sets the whole agenda: every craft and every inquiry, and similarly every action and choice, seems to aim at some good. You go to work to earn money. You earn money to pay rent. You pay rent to have a home. Why do you want a home? Eventually the chain of 'for the sake of' must stop somewhere, or our desires would be empty and pointless.

You will recognise the structure from Days 18 and 19: it is Aristotle's teleology, the idea of a final cause, now turned on human action. There must be some highest good that we want for its own sake and never for the sake of anything else.

Almost everyone agrees on the name of that good, says Aristotle: it is **eudaimonia**. The word is usually translated 'happiness', but that translation misleads. Literally it means something like 'having a good guardian spirit', and in ordinary Greek it meant being blessed, prosperous, faring well. Many scholars prefer 'flourishing' or 'living well'. The difference matters. For us, happiness is often a mood: you can feel happy at 10 a.m. and miserable by lunch. For Aristotle, eudaimonia is a property of a whole life. It is not something you feel but something you do and are.

That is why he can say that, as one swallow does not make a spring, nor does one fine day, so one day or a short time does not make a person blessed and happy. It is also why he was willing to entertain the old Greek saying, attributed to the Athenian statesman Solon, that you should call no man happy until he is dead.

People disagree, Aristotle notes, about what eudaimonia consists in. The crowd says pleasure. Ambitious people say honour. Some say wealth, but wealth is obviously only a means. Honour depends too much on other people. Pleasure alone is a life fit for grazing cattle. To settle the question, we need to know what kind of being a human is.

sections.heading: The Function Argument
sections.body:
Here Aristotle makes his most famous and most controversial move, known as the **function argument** (Book I, chapter 7). The Greek word is *ergon*, meaning function, work or characteristic activity.

The argument runs roughly like this:

1. A flute-player, a sculptor or any craftsman has a function, and their good, their doing well, lies in performing that function well.
2. Eyes, hands and feet each have a function. It would be strange if a human being as such had none.
3. A human's function cannot be mere living, because plants share that (the nutritive soul from Day 19). It cannot be perception, because horses and oxen share that.
4. What is distinctive of humans is the life of the part of the soul that has reason.
5. So the human good is activity of the soul in accordance with reason, done well, which means in accordance with **virtue** (*arete*, excellence).
6. And he adds a crucial qualification: in a complete life.

Notice that *arete* does not mean narrowly moral 'virtue'. It means excellence of any kind: a sharp knife has the *arete* of a knife; a fast horse has the *arete* of a horse. A good human is excellent at being human.

The argument has been attacked ever since. Why assume humans have a function at all, as tools and organs do? Tools get their purpose from their makers and organs from the whole body they serve. And why should the good be what is *distinctive* of us rather than what is most important? Humans are also distinctively capable of elaborate cruelty. Defenders reply that Aristotle is not saying 'whatever is unique is good', but that a thing flourishes by doing well what the kind of thing it is does, and reasoning is central to what humans are.

Aristotle was also realistic. Virtue alone is not quite enough. A person needs some 'external goods': friends, some wealth, decent looks, good children, good birth. He points to King Priam of Troy, who lived well but suffered terrible catastrophes in old age; no one, he says, calls such a man happy. Virtue makes you resilient, but you are not invulnerable. Hold onto this point: the Stoics (Days 25 and 26) will reject it.

sections.heading: Virtue as Habit
sections.body:
Aristotle divides the virtues into two kinds. **Intellectual virtues**, such as wisdom and understanding, grow mostly through teaching. **Virtues of character** (*ethike arete*, from *ethos*, habit), such as courage, generosity and self-control, grow through habit.

This is one of his deepest disagreements with Socrates (Day 9). Socrates held that virtue is knowledge: if you truly knew what was good, you would do it. Aristotle thought this ignored how people actually become good. We do not become brave by reading a definition of courage. We become builders by building and harpists by playing the harp, he says, and in the same way we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, and brave by doing brave acts.

So moral education starts early, before children can understand reasons. It hardly matters a little, he says, whether we are trained in one set of habits or another from childhood; it makes a very great difference, or rather all the difference.

But a virtue is not just an automatic routine. Aristotle defines virtue of character as a **hexis**, a settled state or disposition, concerned with choice, lying in a mean relative to us, determined by reason as a person of practical wisdom would determine it. A truly virtuous act must be done knowingly, chosen for its own sake, and done from a firm and unchanging character.

He adds a wonderful test: pleasure. The person who gives up a luxury and is glad to do so is temperate; the one who gives it up resentfully is merely self-controlled. Real virtue means your feelings have been trained to line up with your reason, so that doing the right thing does not feel like a constant struggle.

In Book VII Aristotle also discusses **akrasia**, weakness of will: knowing what is best and yet doing otherwise. Socrates had denied it was possible. Aristotle, characteristically, takes the everyday phenomenon seriously and tries to explain how desire can cloud knowledge in the moment.

sections.heading: The Golden Mean
sections.body:
The most famous part of Aristotle's ethics is the doctrine of the **mean**, later called the golden mean. Each virtue of character is a midpoint between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency.

- Courage lies between cowardice (too much fear, too little confidence) and rashness (too little fear).
- Generosity lies between stinginess and wastefulness.
- Proper pride lies between small-mindedness and vanity.
- Good temper lies between irascibility and a slavish inability to get angry even when one should.
- Wittiness lies between boorishness and buffoonery.

Three warnings stop this from becoming a bland rule of 'always be moderate'.

First, the mean is **relative to us**, not arithmetical. Aristotle's example is food: if ten pounds is too much for an athlete and two pounds too little, the trainer will not simply prescribe six; the right amount for Milo, a famous wrestler, differs from the right amount for a beginner. The right amount of courage for a firefighter differs from that of an accountant.

Second, the mean concerns not only actions but feelings, and is about responding at the right times, about the right things, toward the right people, for the right reason and in the right way. Sometimes the mean is strong anger: being calm when a child is being bullied is a deficiency, not a virtue.

Third, some actions and feelings have no mean at all. There is no right amount of adultery, theft or murder, and no virtuous level of spite or envy. They are bad in themselves.

Aristotle admits that hitting the mean is hard. There are many ways to miss the target and only one way to hit it. His practical advice: steer away from whichever extreme is more opposed to the mean, and watch for the errors you personally are drawn to, bending yourself the other way as people straighten warped timber.

sections.heading: Practical Wisdom
sections.body:
If the mean is 'what a person of practical wisdom would determine', everything depends on that person. **Phronesis**, practical wisdom, is the intellectual virtue that ties the whole system together (Book VI).

Phronesis is not cleverness, which can serve any goal, including bad ones. Nor is it theoretical wisdom, the knowledge of eternal and unchanging things like mathematics or the heavens. It is the ability to deliberate well about what is good for human life, here, now, in this particular situation. It requires perceiving what a situation calls for, and that perception is learned by experience. That is why, Aristotle says, young people can be brilliant at geometry but are rarely practically wise: they have not lived enough.

This leads to one of his most important methodological claims. Ethics cannot be as precise as mathematics. It is the mark of an educated person, he says, to look for precision in each subject only as far as its nature allows. There is no algorithm that tells you exactly how honest to be with a dying friend. There are good people who see well, and we learn from them.

Character virtue and practical wisdom need each other. Virtue makes the goal right; phronesis finds the right means. A kind person without wisdom blunders; a clever person without virtue becomes a skilled manipulator.

Critics have long pointed to a circularity here. Right action is what the practically wise person would do; the practically wise person is the one who does the right thing. Doesn't that leave beginners with no guidance? Defenders reply that this is simply how expertise works in any field: we recognise good doctors and good teachers before we can define good medicine or teaching, and we learn by apprenticeship. Whether that satisfies you will shape what you think of virtue ethics when it returns in the twentieth century (Day 85).

sections.heading: Friendship and the Contemplative Life
sections.body:
Two of the ten books of the *Ethics*, a fifth of the work, are devoted to **philia**, friendship, which Aristotle calls most necessary for living: no one would choose to live without friends even if he had all other goods.

He distinguishes three kinds, based on what draws people together:

1. **Friendships of utility**, based on usefulness: business contacts, neighbours who swap favours. They dissolve when the usefulness ends.
2. **Friendships of pleasure**, based on enjoyment: drinking companions, people you have fun with. Common among the young, and they shift as tastes change.
3. **Friendships of virtue**, between good people who love each other for who they are, wishing each other well for the other's own sake. These are rare, take time (you must 'eat salt together', as the saying went) and last.

In a true friendship, a friend is, in Aristotle's phrase, 'another self'. We see ourselves better through such a friend and become better together. Friendship is not an optional extra to a good life; it is part of what a good life is.

Then, in Book X, comes a surprise. After nine books on the active, social life of virtue, Aristotle argues that the highest happiness is **contemplation** (*theoria*): the activity of the intellect grasping eternal truths, as in philosophy and science. It is the most continuous, most self-sufficient and most godlike activity, because the unmoved mover itself is pure thinking (Day 18). The life of ethical and political virtue is happy only 'in a secondary degree'.

Scholars have argued for decades over how to fit this with the rest. On the 'dominant' reading, the best life aims at contemplation above all. On the 'inclusive' reading, eudaimonia includes all the goods of virtue, friendship and thought. Many readers see an unresolved tension between Aristotle the citizen and Aristotle the philosopher, which you can test for yourself in the exercise below.

keyQuote.text: For one swallow does not make a spring, nor does one day; and so too one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed and happy.
keyQuote.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7 (1098a18–20), trans. W. D. Ross

modernConnection.title: Positive Psychology, Habit Science and the Two Kinds of Happiness
modernConnection.body:
When psychologists in the late twentieth century began to study well-being scientifically, they ran straight into Aristotle's distinction. Researchers such as Richard Ryan and Edward Deci, and Carol Ryff, contrasted **hedonic** well-being (feeling good, life satisfaction, more pleasure than pain) with **eudaimonic** well-being (purpose, personal growth, autonomy, good relationships). They borrowed Aristotle's word deliberately. Martin Seligman's 'positive psychology' movement, launched around 1998, likewise argued that a good life involves meaning, engagement and relationships, not just positive emotion.

Some of the findings sound like footnotes to the *Ethics*. Pleasure-seeking alone tends to wear off quickly. Strong, close relationships are among the best predictors of long-term well-being; the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed people since 1938, is often summed up by its directors as showing that good relationships keep us happier and healthier. That is Book VIII with a research budget.

Aristotle's claim that character is built by repeated action also anticipates modern habit research. Studies of habit formation suggest that behaviours repeated in stable contexts become increasingly automatic, and therapists use 'behavioural activation', doing the valued action before you feel like it, as a treatment for depression. Act brave to become brave.

And social media gives his friendship taxonomy fresh bite. A feed of hundreds of 'friends' is dominated by friendships of utility (networking) and pleasure (entertainment). Aristotle thought you could have only a few friends of virtue, because such friendship requires time, shared life and intimate knowledge.

But be honest about the gaps. Psychology measures well-being largely through self-reports, so it often slides back toward 'feeling satisfied', which Aristotle would deny is the same as flourishing. A cruel person might report high meaning in life; for Aristotle they could not be eudaimon. Science can tell you what tends to make people feel fulfilled. Whether a life is genuinely *good* is still a philosophical question.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's highest human good, often translated 'happiness' but better understood as flourishing or living well over a complete life.
vocabulary.example: A person can have a miserable afternoon and still be living a life of eudaimonia.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's argument that since a human's distinctive function is rational activity, the human good is rational activity performed excellently, in accordance with virtue.
vocabulary.example: The function argument reasons that just as a good harpist plays well, a good human lives rationally well.

vocabulary.definition: Excellence of any kind; in ethics, the qualities of character and intellect that make a human being good at being human.
vocabulary.example: Sharpness is the arete of a knife; courage and practical wisdom are part of the arete of a person.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that each virtue of character lies between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency, at a point relative to the person and situation.
vocabulary.example: Generosity is the golden mean between stinginess and wasteful extravagance.

vocabulary.definition: The intellectual virtue of deliberating well about what is good for human life in particular situations; it is learned through experience.
vocabulary.example: A nurse with phronesis knows when a patient needs the blunt truth and when they need gentleness first.

vocabulary.definition: A settled state of character formed by habituation, from which actions and feelings reliably flow.
vocabulary.example: Honesty is a hexis: an honest person tells the truth not by accident but because of who they have become.

vocabulary.definition: Weakness of will: knowing what is best and acting against that knowledge, a possibility Socrates denied and Aristotle tried to explain.
vocabulary.example: Promising yourself an early night and then watching four more episodes is a classic case of akrasia.

vocabulary.definition: Friendship or love in a broad sense; Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility, of pleasure and of virtue.
vocabulary.example: Two old friends who would help each other even if nothing could be gained show the highest form of philia.

thinkingExercise.title: Map Your Own Mean
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use Aristotle's tools to audit one area of your character and one of your friendships, as honestly as you can.
steps: Choose one virtue you care about (for example courage, generosity, patience or honesty). Write down the vice of excess and the vice of deficiency on either side of it.
Recall three recent situations where this virtue was called for. For each, mark whether you hit the mean, overshot or undershot. Which extreme are you more naturally drawn toward?
Following Aristotle's 'bend the timber' advice, design one small action you could repeat daily for two weeks to nudge yourself toward the mean.
Now list five people you consider friends. Classify each friendship as mainly utility, pleasure or virtue. Does the result surprise you?
Finally, write a paragraph answering: if you had to choose, would you rather have a life that feels happy or a life that is eudaimon in Aristotle's sense? Are they really different?

summary: All human action aims at some good, and the highest good, wanted for its own sake, is eudaimonia: flourishing across a complete life, not a passing mood.
The function argument says the human good is rational activity done excellently, in accordance with virtue, though virtue needs some external goods and luck.
Virtues of character are built by habit; we become just by doing just acts, and real virtue means our feelings come to agree with reason.
Each virtue is a mean relative to us between excess and deficiency, but some actions, like murder, have no mean.
Practical wisdom (phronesis) finds the right action in particular situations; ethics cannot be as precise as mathematics.
Friendship of virtue is part of the good life, yet Book X ranks contemplation highest, a tension scholars still debate.

quiz.question: Why do many scholars prefer 'flourishing' to 'happiness' as a translation of eudaimonia?
options: Because eudaimonia refers only to physical health
Because eudaimonia describes the quality of a whole life of activity, not a passing feeling
Because Aristotle thought pleasure was always bad
Because eudaimonia was a technical term invented by Aristotle
quiz.explanation: Eudaimonia is a property of a complete life lived well, which is why one fine day does not make a person eudaimon. Aristotle did not think pleasure was always bad, and the word was ordinary Greek, not his invention.

quiz.question: In the function argument, why can't the human good be mere nourishment and growth?
options: Because the gods forbid it
Because humans do not need nourishment
Because plants share that capacity, so it is not distinctive of humans
Because nourishment is a vice of excess
quiz.explanation: Aristotle seeks what is distinctive of humans. Nutrition belongs to all living things and perception to all animals, so the human function must involve reason.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, how do we acquire virtues of character such as courage?
options: By memorising correct definitions of each virtue
By being born with them
By contemplating the Form of the Good
By repeatedly performing courageous acts until they become habitual
quiz.explanation: We become brave by doing brave acts, as builders become builders by building. This contrasts with Socrates' view that virtue is knowledge and with Plato's Forms.

quiz.question: A firefighter and an office worker face very different dangers. What does Aristotle's phrase 'the mean relative to us' imply?
options: The right level of courage depends on the person and situation, not on a fixed midpoint
Both should feel exactly the same amount of fear
Courage is only a virtue for soldiers
The office worker cannot be courageous at all
quiz.explanation: Like Milo the wrestler's diet, the mean is not arithmetical. What is right depends on who you are and what the situation calls for.

quiz.question: Which of these, according to Aristotle, has NO mean?
options: Anger
Spending money
Envy
Joking
quiz.explanation: Aristotle says some feelings and actions, such as envy, spite, adultery, theft and murder, are bad in themselves; there is no right amount of them. Anger, spending and joking each have a virtuous mean.

quiz.question: Two colleagues get along well only because they help each other hit sales targets. When one changes jobs, they never speak again. Which kind of friendship was this?
options: Friendship of virtue
Friendship of pleasure
Friendship of contemplation
Friendship of utility
quiz.explanation: A friendship based on mutual usefulness is a friendship of utility, which dissolves when the usefulness ends. There is no 'friendship of contemplation' in Aristotle's scheme.

quiz.question: What is phronesis?
options: Theoretical knowledge of eternal truths
The ability to deliberate well about what to do in particular situations
Cleverness that can serve any goal, good or bad
A vice of excessive caution
quiz.explanation: Phronesis is practical wisdom about human life in concrete cases. Aristotle distinguishes it from theoretical wisdom and from mere cleverness, which can serve evil ends.

quiz.question: Aristotle believed virtue alone guarantees happiness, no matter what misfortunes strike.
quiz.explanation: Aristotle says external goods matter, and that someone who suffers Priam's catastrophes is not called happy. The Stoics would later take the opposite view.

quiz.question: Aristotle thought ethics should aim for the same precision as mathematics.
quiz.explanation: He says an educated person seeks only as much precision as the subject allows, and ethics deals with particulars that resist exact rules.

quiz.question: In Book X of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle ranks the contemplative life as the highest form of happiness.
quiz.explanation: Book X calls contemplation the most self-sufficient and godlike activity and ranks the life of practical virtue as happy 'in a secondary degree'.

goDeeper.body:
Two big debates are worth exploring once you have the basics. The first is the 'dominant versus inclusive' controversy about eudaimonia. In a well-known 1974 essay, 'Aristotle on Eudaimonia', J. L. Ackrill argued that when Aristotle calls eudaimonia the most complete end, he means an inclusive good that contains all intrinsically valuable activities, virtue, friendship and contemplation together. Others, such as Richard Kraut in *Aristotle on the Human Good*, argue that Book X is the culmination, not an afterthought, and that happiness is identified with one dominant activity, contemplation, with the rest valuable in relation to it. The answer affects how we read the whole work: is the ideal person a wise citizen or a philosopher who withdraws to think?

The second debate is about luck. Aristotle admits that a good life is vulnerable to fortune, from what family you are born into to whether catastrophe strikes. Martha Nussbaum's *The Fragility of Goodness* argues that this vulnerability is not a flaw in his theory but its great insight, connecting it to the Greek tragedians you will meet tomorrow. The twentieth-century philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel coined the phrase 'moral luck' for the troubling way our moral standing seems to depend on things outside our control.

Finally, notice that Aristotle's ethics is addressed to a privileged audience: free, male, propertied Athenians with leisure. Can his ideal of flourishing be extended to everyone, or does it depend on others doing the labour? That question leads straight into Day 21.

readings.title: Nicomachean Ethics, Books I–II and VIII
readings.author: Aristotle
readings.note: Book I covers eudaimonia and the function argument, Book II habit and the mean, Book VIII friendship. Try Roger Crisp's (Cambridge) or Terence Irwin's (Hackett) translation.

readings.title: Aristotle's Way: How Ancient Wisdom Can Change Your Life
readings.author: Edith Hall
readings.note: An accessible and personal guide by a leading classicist, applying the Ethics to everyday decisions.

readings.title: The Fragility of Goodness
readings.author: Martha C. Nussbaum
readings.note: For the ambitious: chapters 11–12 on Aristotle's view that a good life is exposed to luck.

readings.title: On Virtue Ethics
readings.author: Rosalind Hursthouse
readings.note: A modern philosophical defence of Aristotle-inspired ethics, including a response to the 'circularity' worry.

questions: Is it fair that, on Aristotle's view, someone struck by terrible misfortune cannot be fully eudaimon, however virtuous they are?
Can there be a person who is brilliant and kind but lacks practical wisdom? What would they get wrong?
Does the internet make friendships of virtue easier, harder, or no different to form?
